topic: firing schedule and packing of a small gas kiln in a pottery workshop

provenance.author: subagent-en-a
provenance.notes: independent English scenario, not a translation; five sentences per turn

a: Here are five cone temperatures in degrees Celsius: 1186, 1222, 1240, 1063 and 1101.
Sort those five figures from lowest to highest and keep them in whole degrees.
Give me the difference between the lowest and the highest of the five.
Then work out the mean of the five temperatures, rounded to the nearest whole degree.
Tell me which of the five figures sit above that mean value and which sit below.
base: The workshop kiln is a small gas updraught, about six cubic feet, with two burners.
I have been firing bisque overnight and glaze the next day, but the results wander.
One shelf comes out fine and the shelf above it is under fired by a clear margin.
The kiln sits in an open shed, so the weather gets into it more than I would like.
Where should I look first for the cause of that difference between shelves?

a: Sorted from lowest to highest the five temperatures run 1063, 1101, 1186, 1222 and 1240.
The difference between the lowest and the highest of the five figures is 177 degrees.
The five temperatures add up to 5812 degrees in all, which gives a mean of 1162.
Three of the figures sit above that mean, namely 1186, 1222 and 1240 degrees.
The two that sit below the mean are 1063 and 1101 degrees, as whole values.
base: A difference between shelves in an updraught kiln is usually about how the flame travels.
Packing too tightly at the bottom starves the upper half of moving heat.
Leave a clear channel up one side and keep the top shelf well below the flue.
How far apart are the shelves, and are the posts the same height throughout the stack?
An open shed will also cool one side of the kiln whenever the wind gets up.

a: The kiln goes from twenty degrees to 1240 degrees over a firing of eleven hours.
Work out the average rise in degrees per hour, rounded to one decimal place.
The last two hours are held at a rise of only fifty degrees per hour.
Work out how much of the climb happens in the first nine hours of the firing.
Then give me the average rise per hour across those first nine hours alone.
base: The shelves are at nine inch spacings, and the posts are a mixture of nine and twelve.
I have been packing tight because I want the kiln full before I light it.
The flue is at the top centre and the top shelf is maybe four inches below it.
That may be the whole story, and it would explain the pattern I keep seeing.
The wind does come straight through the shed from the west most afternoons.

a: The full climb is 1220 degrees over eleven hours, which averages 110.9 degrees per hour.
The last two hours at fifty degrees an hour account for 100 degrees of that climb.
That leaves 1120 degrees of the total rise to happen in the first nine hours.
Dividing 1120 by nine gives an average of 124.4 degrees per hour, to one decimal.
So the early part climbs faster than the firing taken as a whole.
base: Nine inch posts under a twelve inch gap will lean, and a leaning stack blocks the draught.
Use posts of one height per layer and keep the shelves flat across the whole stack.
Four inches under the flue is too close, because the heat leaves before it spreads.
Drop the top shelf to six or seven inches and the upper half will even out.
A screen on the west side of the shed will take the worst of the wind off.

a: Here is the shelf load: four bowls, nine mugs, two jugs, six plates and three lidded jars.
Add those up and tell me the total number of pots on the shelf.
Split them into open forms and closed forms, counting the jars as closed.
Give me the two group totals with the larger of the two groups listed first.
Then tell me what share of the load the closed forms make, as a percentage.
base: I can change the posts easily enough, and the screen is a morning's work with pallets.
What I am less sure about is the glaze itself, which crawls on the thicker pieces.
It is a matt white that behaves perfectly on test tiles and badly on the jars.
The jars are the pieces I bisque hardest, because the lids need a good fit.
Could the bisque temperature be doing something to how the glaze sits on the wall?

a: The shelf holds twenty-four pots in total, adding four, nine, two, six and three together.
The open forms are the bowls, the mugs and the plates, giving nineteen pots in all.
The closed forms are the jugs and the lidded jars, giving five pots in all.
Listing the larger group first gives nineteen open forms and then five closed forms.
Five pots out of twenty-four is 20.8 per cent of the shelf load.
base: A hard bisque closes the wall and leaves less for the glaze to key into.
On a matt white that shows up as crawling, especially on a vertical surface.
Test tiles lie because they are flat and the glaze has nowhere to run.
Bisque the jars with everything else and take the fit of the lids at the glaze firing.
If the wall still refuses the glaze, thin it slightly and put it on in two passes.

a: Take the eleven hour firing and split it into four named stages as evenly as you can.
Give each stage a start hour and an end hour, running from zero to eleven.
The stages will not be equal, since eleven hours does not divide evenly by four.
Put the longer stages at the start and keep the shorter ones at the end.
Then list the four stages on four lines with their hours in brackets.
base: Thinning it and putting it on in two passes is something I have not tried.
I usually dip once and let it be, because a second dip lifts the first.
The other thing I want to sort out is when to close the damper on the way up.
At the moment I go by colour, which works until the light in the shed changes.
Is there a steadier marker than colour to work from on a kiln this size?

a: The four stages come out as three hours, three hours, three hours and two hours.
Stage one runs from hour zero to hour three, and stage two from three to six.
Stage three runs from hour six to hour nine, and stage four from nine to eleven.
The longer stages sit at the start and the two hour stage sits at the end.
Those are the four lines, each with its start hour and its end hour.
base: Cones are the steadier marker, because they read heat work rather than colour alone.
Set a low cone in the spy hole and close the damper when it starts to bend.
Colour in an open shed will always shift with the light outside the door.
A pyrometer helps with the climb but tells you nothing about soaking time.
Use the two together and the damper stops being a matter of pure guesswork.

a: Write out the packing order for the shelf, from the lowest layer to the highest.
Number the layers from one to four and keep each layer on a single line.
Put the plates on the bottom layer and the lidded jars on the top layer.
Then mark which layers need nine inch posts and which need twelve inch posts.
Keep the whole thing plain with no explanation between the numbered layers.
base: That settles the damper, and I can put a cone in the spy hole tomorrow.
The last loose end is the cooling, which I have never controlled at all.
I simply shut everything down at the top and open the door the next morning.
The matt white is supposed to like a slow cool, according to the recipe.
Would holding some heat on the way down change what I am getting?

a: Layer one holds the plates, layer two the bowls, layer three the mugs and jugs.
Layer four holds the three lidded jars at the top of the stack.
Layers one and two take the twelve inch posts, because the plates and bowls stand tall.
Layers three and four take the nine inch posts, which suits mugs, jugs and jars.
That is the packing order set out plain from the lowest layer to the highest.
base: Holding heat on the way down is exactly what a matt white wants.
Close everything tight and let it fall to about a thousand degrees on its own.
Then put one burner back on low and hold there for half an hour.
Matt surfaces come from crystals that grow in that band as the kiln cools.
Opening the door hot will craze the glaze and undo the whole slow cool.
